By nightfall the British army had 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 dead, its worst day ever. Look at the timeline of the war in the west. How did it come to this?

explain.say: Now let me show you a trench in 3D, as it was on the Western Front. Look at the parapet of sandbags, the fire step, the duckboards, the dugout, and the barbed wire facing no man's land. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: Trench warfare and total war: the Western Front and the home front

explain.say: Look at the cutaway of a trench. Soldiers stood on the fire step behind sandbags, slept in dugouts and lived on duckboards above the mud. In front lay no man's land, barbed wire and craters. Machine guns and artillery made defence far stronger than attack, so from late 1914 the armies were stuck. Why is crossing open ground so deadly?

explain.say: Now the map. The Western Front ran about 700 kilometres from the Belgian coast to Switzerland. At Verdun in 1916, French and German armies fought for ten months; at Ypres, gas was used in 1915. Beyond Europe, Gallipoli failed, and over a million Indian soldiers and about 140,000 Chinese labourers served. Why call it a world war?

This was total war: whole societies mobilised. Watch the chain. Conscription called up millions of men, women worked in munitions factories, a British naval blockade brought hunger to Germany, and governments controlled news and food. Which link do you think changed women's lives most?

stages.label: Social change
stages.note: Some women win the vote in 1918.

explain.say: See the sizes, all estimates: about nine to ten million soldiers died, plus millions of civilians. Each was someone's child. Historians once said British soldiers were lions led by donkeys; others, like Gary Sheffield, describe a learning curve that won in 1918. Thoughtful work. Exam tip: use a specific battle as evidence for either view.

faq.q: Why did the First World War become a trench stalemate?
faq.a: After the Battle of the Marne in September 1914 stopped Germany's advance, both sides dug in. Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made defence much stronger than attack, so neither side could break through for years.
asks: Why did the war get stuck?

faq.q: What happened on the first day of the Somme?
faq.a: On 1 July 1916 British and French forces attacked after a week-long bombardment that failed to cut the wire or destroy German dugouts. The British army suffered 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 killed, its worst single day.
asks: What was the Battle of Verdun?
How many died at the Somme?

faq.a: A war in which a state mobilises its whole society and economy: conscription, war industry, rationing, propaganda and control of the press, and in which civilians and their economies also become targets, for example through blockade.

faq.q: Were British soldiers lions led by donkeys?
faq.a: That popular view blames incompetent generals for huge losses. Historians such as Gary Sheffield argue that the British army learned new tactics, combining artillery, tanks and infantry, and helped win in 1918, though the cost was terrible.
asks: What is the learning curve debate?

faq.q: Who fought on the Western Front from outside Europe?
faq.a: Soldiers and workers came from across empires: over a million Indian soldiers served in the war, and troops from Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Africa and the Caribbean fought, while about 140,000 Chinese labourers worked behind the lines.
asks: Did Indian soldiers fight in the First World War?

facts: On 1 July 1916 the British army had 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 killed.
The Battle of Verdun lasted from February to December 1916.
The armistice came into force at 11 am on 11 November 1918.

quiz.say: Of 57,470 British casualties on the first day of the Somme, 19,240 were killed. About what fraction is that?
quiz.why: 19,240 divided by 57,470 is about 0.33, one third.

quiz.say: Why did defence beat attack on the Western Front?
quiz.show: Defence was stronger mainly because of…
quiz.why: Machine guns and artillery cut down attackers held up by barbed wire.

wrong.1: Armies were huge; numbers were not the problem.
wrong.2: Cavalry was largely useless against machine guns and wire.
